title: Không gian riêng của thiếu niên · Agree / Disagree
prompt: Some people believe that giving teenagers a reasonable degree of privacy at home is a sensible approach. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

source.detail: Bài luyện mở rộng biên soạn riêng cho năm 2026. Tham khảo các nhóm chủ đề trong forecast công khai; tình huống, bài mẫu và phân tích được viết mới.
source.disclaimer: Không xác nhận đề này đã xuất hiện hoặc sẽ xuất hiện trong kỳ thi. Các chủ đề ngách được bổ sung để mở rộng phạm vi luyện tập; không gán xác suất ra thi.

keywords: Không gian riêng của thiếu niên Tôn trọng không gian riêng có thể khiến thiếu niên sẵn lòng tự nguyện chia sẻ lo lắng thật bởi vì người trẻ ít lý do giấu lỗi thông thường khi chia sẻ không tự động dẫn đến kiểm tra xâm phạm. Minh họa: Thiếu niên có thể trao đổi tin nhắn gây buồn với người cha hoặc mẹ thường xin phép trước khi vào phòng. Không suy rộng từ ví dụ thành bảo đảm thành công cho tất cả.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
paragraphs: Adolescence changes the balance between parental protection and private space, and routine surveillance can make that adjustment unnecessarily adversarial. I broadly agree with the proposal, but my support rests on a clear distinction: privacy is a presumption of trust rather than immunity from proportionate protection.

Respecting private space can make teenagers more willing to share genuine concerns voluntarily. The mechanism is straightforward: young people have less reason to hide ordinary mistakes when disclosure does not automatically invite intrusive inspection. For example, a teenager may discuss an upsetting message with a parent who normally asks permission before entering the bedroom. Trust is especially fragile when an ordinary disagreement is treated as proof that a young person has forfeited all private space. Permission to ask for help should remain open after an ordinary disagreement.

Absolute privacy can prevent timely intervention when there are credible signs of exploitation or self-neglect. Families should establish clear safety exceptions and explain any necessary intervention rather than conducting routine secret searches. A clear agreement about knocking, private messages and emergencies gives both sides expectations that can be discussed before conflict occurs. Secret inspection may reveal a problem once, but if it destroys future disclosure, parents can lose access to the information most important for protecting their child. This qualification is essential because privacy is a presumption of trust rather than immunity from proportionate protection.

I support a presumption of privacy for teenagers, because respectful boundaries can make voluntary disclosure more likely. Credible safety concerns justify proportionate intervention, but they should not become a permanent excuse for secret searches that destroy the trust on which ordinary parental guidance depends.
